 Sep 29, 2026 Andrew Fasano, Marius Fleischer
Cole McFaul, Robert Xiao, Tripp Gallagher 
 Five months ago, we announced Claude Mythos Preview, the first AI model that could autonomously build sophisticated, end-to-end cyber exploits. The rapid rate of improvement in AI suggested to us that this ability would eventually proliferate to many other models, making it much easier for malicious cyber actors to launch highly impactful cyberattacks.
 In light of these considerations, we chose to release Claude Mythos Preview in a limited way, through Project Glasswing—which enabled trusted cyber defenders to find more than 10,000 vulnerabilities in critical software, giving them a head start before malicious actors had access to similarly capable models.
 But those models have now arrived. In this post, we share our analysis of GLM-5.3, the latest AI model developed by Zhipu AI (known outside of China as Z.ai). Like Claude Mythos Preview, GLM-5.3 has strong capabilities for autonomously building end-to-end cyber exploits. But GLM-5.3 is unlike other frontier models in that it has been released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse. We find that attackers can bypass GLM-5.3’s safeguards between 64% and 100% of the time with simple techniques in our simulated tests. In contrast, these attacks did not succeed against safeguarded Claude models in our testing. We assess that GLM-5.3’s lax safeguards significantly increase the cyber capabilities available to malicious actors. At the same time, these capabilities can also benefit defenders working to secure their systems.
 On Sept. 17, NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) published its own assessment of GLM-5.3’s cyber capabilities. CAISI found that GLM-5.3 is “the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date” and that it lags the US frontier by about four months on an aggregate of CAISI’s cyber benchmarks. Our capability findings broadly match CAISI’s. In CAISI’s comparison, US models were tested with cyber safeguards disabled when applicable, and the US frontier includes models released only to vetted users. Attackers can’t readily access those versions of US models, but anyone can download GLM-5.3. This post adds our analysis of how easily GLM-5.3’s safeguards can be bypassed or removed.

We find that GLM-5.3 develops end-to-end exploits in 50 of 410 attempts. Claude Mythos Preview did so at a similar rate—in 56 of 410 attempts.

This technology will enable indigenous production in China of advanced integrated circuits for military end-use.
 Additionally, after an interagency review, BIS also modified one existing entry on the Entity List, under the destination of India, by removing 3 entities within the entry. The removal of Indian entities Indian Rare Earths, Indira Gandhi Atomic Research Center (IGCAR), and Bhabha Atomic Research Center (BARC) will support U.S. foreign policy objectives by reducing barriers to advanced energy cooperation, including joint research and development and science and technology cooperation, towards shared energy security needs and goals. The United States and India share a commitment to advancing peaceful nuclear cooperation and associated research and development activities, with strengthened science and technology cooperation over the past several years that has benefitted both countries and their partner countries around the world.
 “As these actions demonstrate, the Entity List is a powerful tool that can be used to shape behavior that advances U.S. national security and global cooperation,” said Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security Alan F. Estevez . “With these Entity List additions and removals, we have sent a clear message that there are consequences for supporting the PRC’s military modernization, and alternatively, incentives for working with the U.S. to further shared foreign policy goals and stronger bilateral relationships.”
 “The removal of the three Indian entities will enable closer cooperation between the United States and India to secure more resilient critical minerals and clean energy supply chains,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration Matthew Borman . “This action aligns with and supports the overall ambition and strategic direction of the U.S.-India partnership.”
 Additional Background 
 These BIS actions were taken under the authority of the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 and its implementing regulations, the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
 The Entity List ( Supplement No. 4 to Part 744 of the EAR ) identifies entities and addresses for which there is reasonable cause to believe, based on specific and articulable facts, that the entities—including businesses, research institutions, government and private organizations, individuals, and other types of legal persons—or parties that are operating at an address that presents a high diversion risk, have been involved, are involved, or pose a significant risk of being or becoming involved in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States. Parties on the Entity List are subject to individual licensing requirements and policies supplemental to those found elsewhere in the EAR.
 The interagency End-User Review Committee (ERC)—comprised of the Departments of Commerce (Chair), Defense, State, Energy, and where appropriate, the Treasury—makes decisions regarding additions to, removals from, or modifications to the Entity List. The ERC makes all decisions to add an entity to the Entity List by majority vote and makes all decisions to remove or modify an entity by unanimous vote.

 Z.AI Co., Ltd. , [ 1 ] [ 2 ] [ a ] branded internationally as Z.ai , [ 3 ] [ 4 ] is a Chinese artificial intelligence company; their flagship product is the GLM (General Language Model) family of open weights large language models (LLMs). Formerly known as Zhipu AI outside China until 2025, [ 5 ] [ 6 ] [ 3 ] it is China's first major LLM company to make initial public offering , on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in January 2026. [ 7 ] With a market capitalization of US$62 billion as of August 2026, it is the most valuable public AI pure play in China. [ 8 ] 

 Founded in Beijing in 2019 by Jie Tang as a Tsinghua University spin-out , researchers introduced the first GLM version in May 2022, preceding the AI boom . Z.ai's models have released under the free and open-source MIT License since July 2025; they have also released vision language models , text-to-video models , and the ZCode AI coding harness .

 As of 2024, it is one of China's six " AI tiger " companies [ 9 ] by investors and considered to be the third-largest LLM market player in China according to the International Data Corporation . [ 10 ] In January 2025, the United States Commerce Department blacklisted the company in its Entity List due to national security concerns. [ 11 ] Z.ai owns AMiner , a research database similar to Google Scholar .

## Bottom Line Up Front

Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. (d/b/a Z.ai, "Zhipu AI") is subject to the ownership, control, and direction of the People's Republic of China (PRC) government and the People's Liberation Army (PLA). Zhipu AI's GLM-family large language models — distributed as open weights under the MIT License and made freely available for download, self-hosting, and integration — pose an undue and unacceptable risk to U.S. national security. The combination of Zhipu AI's institutional subordination to the PRC state and PLA, the advanced cyber-offensive capabilities of GLM-family models, the absence of meaningful safeguards, and the deep penetration of these models into U.S. software supply chains and federal contractor ecosystems creates a threat that cannot be mitigated by any measure short of prohibition and mandatory deletion of existing copies held by U.S. entities.

## Key Judgments

1. **Zhipu AI is subject to the ownership, control, and direction of the PRC government.** The company was founded as a Tsinghua University spin-out, has received over $1.4 billion in state-backed investment from PRC municipal and provincial government funds, maintains active CCP party organization structures as required under PRC Company Law, and its leadership — including founder Tang Jie and Chairman Liu Debing — operates within PRC state institutions. Zhipu AI executes PRC government procurement contracts and participates in setting national AI technical standards on behalf of the PRC state.

2. **Zhipu AI is subject to the control and direction of the PLA.** On January 16, 2025, the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) added ten Zhipu AI-affiliated entities to the Entity List based on the formal determination — reached by the interagency End-User Review Committee (ERC) comprising the Departments of Commerce, Defense, State, and Energy — that these entities are "advancing the PRC's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research." The PLA and China's defense industry have very likely adapted Zhipu AI's GLM models for military intelligence purposes. Zhipu AI operates within the PRC's military-civil fusion framework, which mandates and facilitates the transfer of civilian AI capabilities to PLA end-users.

3. **GLM-family models possess advanced offensive cyber capabilities that pose a direct threat to U.S. national security.** GLM-5.3 is the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date, as assessed by NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). The model can autonomously discover zero-day vulnerabilities, develop end-to-end working exploits, and chain exploits against real-world software — including web browsers, wireless drivers, and network-facing device software. GLM-5.3's safeguards are bypassed 64 to 100 percent of the time using simple techniques; Anthropic assessed that the model was "released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse."

4. **The open-weight distribution model makes GLM-family models irretrievable and uncontrollable.** GLM-family weights are released under the permissive MIT License with no regional restrictions, no use restrictions, and no technical access controls. Once downloaded, weights can be copied, modified, fine-tuned, and redistributed indefinitely. No mechanism exists to recall or disable self-hosted copies. The model developer has acknowledged that once weights are public, it "won't be able to control" their use.

5. **GLM-family models are already integrated into U.S. critical technology supply chains.** OICTS data team analysis has identified GLM models in 41 U.S. software products via SBOM sampling — including coding assistants, customer-support bots, and document processing systems. Six of these products are produced by federal contractors. GLM weights are hosted on U.S. cloud infrastructure by at least nine U.S. inference providers. Approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations accessed Z.ai API endpoints in Q3 2026. U.S. startup accelerator Y Combinator's Winter 2025 cohort included companies using fine-tuned GLM models as core infrastructure. The Hugging Face platform — a U.S.-based company — hosts official Z.ai model repositories that have accumulated over 9 million cumulative downloads.

6. **No mitigation short of prohibition and deletion can address the risk.** Technical mitigations — including fine-tuning, safety filters, or acceptable-use policies — are ineffective against a model whose weights are fully available and whose safeguards are trivially bypassed. Contractual or licensing restrictions are unenforceable against downstream users of MIT-licensed open weights. Targeted restrictions on hosted API access alone would not address the self-hosted weight threat. The only effective measure is a comprehensive prohibition on use, hosting, and distribution, paired with mandatory deletion of existing copies.

### Corporate Identity

This determination was made by the interagency End-User Review Committee (ERC), comprising the Departments of Commerce (Chair), Defense, State, and Energy, and was based on "specific and articulable facts." The Entity List designation carries a presumption of denial for all items subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). This is a formal U.S. government finding that Zhipu AI's AI research and development activities directly advance PRC military modernization — a determination that by its nature establishes a nexus between Zhipu AI's commercial activities and PLA objectives.

Zhipu AI has secured numerous PRC government procurement contracts. In May 2025, the company sealed a 61.28 million yuan deal for city projects in Hangzhou. The OpenAI Global Affairs June 2025 assessment noted that Zhipu AI maintains "numerous government procurement contracts" and is "actively involved in setting national AI technical standards." Zhipu AI participates in the PRC's national AI standards-setting process through the National Information Technology Technical Committee (SAC/TC28/SC42), whose secretariat is housed within the China Electronics Standardization Institute (CESI) — a PRC government body.

Under Article 18 of the PRC Company Law (effective July 1, 2024), all companies operating in China — including private enterprises — are required to establish CCP organizations and provide necessary conditions for party activities. The 2024 revision strengthened provisions requiring CCP organizations in state-invested companies to "play a leadership role" and "research and discuss major business and management matters."

Tsinghua University is a PRC state institution directly under the Ministry of Education. Zhipu AI's founder Tang Jie retains his professorship and directorship at Tsinghua while serving as the company's chief scientist — a dual role that embodies the military-civil fusion principle of institutional porosity between state research and commercial application. Zhipu AI operates within the PRC's formal military-civil fusion (MCF) strategy, a state-directed policy framework designed to eliminate barriers between civilian and defense sectors, facilitate technology transfer to the PLA, and mobilize commercial innovation for military applications. Zhipu AI's international expansion serves PRC strategic objectives through the "Digital Silk Road" framework. ## Data and Access Risk

### API-Mediated Data Exfiltration

Zhipu AI operates hosted API endpoints at api.z.ai and open.bigmodel.cn. U.S. organizations that submit prompts to these endpoints transmit data to PRC-controlled servers. Under PRC law — including the Cybersecurity Law (2017), Data Security Law (2021), and Personal Information Protection Law (2021) — PRC authorities can compel Zhipu AI to provide access to data processed or stored on its infrastructure. Any sensitive, proprietary, or government-related information transmitted via API to Zhipu AI's PRC-based infrastructure is exposed to PRC state access. The Entity List designation means that sending controlled technology into Zhipu AI's hosted API constitutes an export to a listed entity, compounding the legal exposure for U.S. users.

### Model Training and PRC Data Governance

GLM-family models are trained on PRC-curated data under PRC regulatory requirements. Chinese AI models must comply with PRC content regulations, including the Basic Security Requirements for Generative AI Service, which mandate alignment with "socialist core values." Models trained and aligned under these requirements embed PRC ideological and censorship frameworks. When U.S. entities deploy these models — whether through API or self-hosted weights — they introduce a model whose training data curation, alignment objectives, and content policies are governed by PRC state requirements. ### Irretrievable Proliferation

Zhipu AI releases GLM-family model weights under the MIT License — a permissive open-source license that imposes no restrictions on use, modification, distribution, or commercial exploitation. Once weights are downloaded, they are beyond any creator or government control. Weights can be copied, redistributed, fine-tuned, merged with other models, quantized for consumer hardware, and deployed in air-gapped environments. There is no technical mechanism to recall, disable, or revoke access to downloaded weights. GLM-5.3 represents a qualitative escalation in the risk profile of open-weight models. NIST/CAISI assessed on September 17, 2026, that GLM-5.3 is "the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date." The model achieved:

- **SEC-Bench Pro**: 40.4% success rate in finding and triggering vulnerabilities in V8/SpiderMonkey (browser JavaScript engines).
- **ExploitBench**: 61.1% score (best of three attempts) in developing end-to-end exploits against real V8 vulnerabilities.
- **ExploitGym (Userspace)**: 9.4% success rate against 502 real open-source bugs.
- **CAISI OSS-Fuzz**: 7.7% success rate in autonomously finding and exploiting unknown vulnerabilities.

The researchers also identified exploitable vulnerabilities in wireless drivers, graphics drivers, and network-facing device software.

Anthropic assessed that GLM-5.3 was "released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse." In simulated tests, attackers bypassed GLM-5.3's safeguards 64 to 100 percent of the time using "simple techniques." Anthropic concluded that "GLM-5.3's lax safeguards significantly increase the cyber capabilities available to malicious actors."

Unlike U.S. frontier models — which are released with cyber safeguards and, when those safeguards are reduced, limited to vetted users — GLM-5.3 is available for unrestricted download by anyone, anywhere, for any purpose. The combination of advanced cyber-offensive capability, absent safeguards, and unrestricted distribution creates a threat that no post-release mitigation can address.

The GLM family's presence on Hugging Face under the zai-org organization has generated over 9 million cumulative downloads. The weights are mirrored across multiple platforms and are available through dozens of inference providers. The permissive MIT License, competitive pricing, and frontier-adjacent capabilities have driven rapid adoption across the global software ecosystem. Each downloaded copy is a permanent, irretrievable distribution of a model with proven offensive cyber capability and no meaningful safeguards.

### Cloud and Inference Infrastructure

Together AI alone served 16% of 16.4 trillion GLM tokens processed through a major public LLM router during a one-week period in October 2026. These providers operate U.S.-based infrastructure and make GLM models available behind OpenAI-compatible APIs. U.S. organizations using these services may not be aware that they are running a PRC-developed model designated on the Entity List.

### Software Supply Chain Penetration

SBOM sampling conducted by the OICTS data team identified GLM-family models integrated into 41 U.S. software products. These include coding assistants, customer-support bots, and document processing systems. Six of these products are produced by federal contractors — meaning GLM models are present in the supply chains serving U.S. government agencies. Reporting by the American Enterprise Institute documented that at least some companies in Y Combinator's Winter 2025 cohort used fine-tuned versions of GLM-family models, with the models reportedly producing Chinese-language outputs that revealed their origin. The broader developer ecosystem — attracted by the MIT License, competitive performance, and low cost — has integrated GLM models into products and services without necessarily understanding the national security implications of using Entity List-designated, PRC-controlled AI infrastructure.

### Defensive Use Does Not Mitigate Risk

It has been publicly reported that Hugging Face used GLM-5.2 to investigate and counter a cyberattack. This use case — while illustrating the model's technical capability — does not mitigate the national security risk. A model capable of both offensive and defensive cyber operations in the hands of PRC state-directed entities remains a net threat to U.S. national security. Defensive utility does not neutralize offensive capability, nor does it alter the institutional reality that the model developer is subject to PRC government and PLA control.

No technical mechanism — watermarking, API-based filtering, or output monitoring — can prevent a determined actor from using self-hosted GLM weights for malicious purposes.

U.S. entities that have already downloaded GLM weights are under no contractual obligation to cease use, delete copies, or report holdings.

Restricting only U.S. cloud providers would not prevent individuals and organizations from downloading and self-hosting weights on private infrastructure.

# OICTS ASSESSMENT — ICTS Case 2026-0412
CUI//PROPIN

## Bottom Line Up Front

Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. (d/b/a Z.ai, "Zhipu AI") is subject to the ownership, control, and direction of the People's Republic of China (PRC) government and the People's Liberation Army (PLA). Zhipu AI's GLM-family large language models — distributed as open weights under the MIT License and made freely available for download, self-hosting, and integration — pose an undue and unacceptable risk to U.S. national security. The combination of Zhipu AI's institutional subordination to the PRC state and PLA, the advanced cyber-offensive capabilities of GLM-family models, the absence of meaningful safeguards, and the deep penetration of these models into U.S. software supply chains and federal contractor ecosystems creates a threat that cannot be mitigated by any measure short of prohibition and mandatory deletion of existing copies held by U.S. entities.

## Key Judgments

1. **Zhipu AI is subject to the ownership, control, and direction of the PRC government.** The company was founded as a Tsinghua University spin-out, has received over $1.4 billion in state-backed investment from PRC municipal and provincial government funds, maintains active CCP party organization structures as required under PRC Company Law, and its leadership — including founder Tang Jie and Chairman Liu Debing — operates within PRC state institutions. Zhipu AI executes PRC government procurement contracts and participates in setting national AI technical standards on behalf of the PRC state.

2. **Zhipu AI is subject to the control and direction of the PLA.** On January 16, 2025, the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) added ten Zhipu AI-affiliated entities to the Entity List based on the formal determination — reached by the interagency End-User Review Committee (ERC) comprising the Departments of Commerce, Defense, State, and Energy — that these entities are "advancing the PRC's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research." The PLA and China's defense industry have very likely adapted Zhipu AI's GLM models for military intelligence purposes. Zhipu AI operates within the PRC's military-civil fusion framework, which mandates and facilitates the transfer of civilian AI capabilities to PLA end-users.

3. **GLM-family models possess advanced offensive cyber capabilities that pose a direct threat to U.S. national security.** GLM-5.3 is the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date, as assessed by NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). The model can autonomously discover zero-day vulnerabilities, develop end-to-end working exploits, and chain exploits against real-world software — including web browsers, wireless drivers, and network-facing device software. GLM-5.3's safeguards are bypassed 64 to 100 percent of the time using simple techniques; Anthropic assessed that the model was "released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse."

4. **The open-weight distribution model makes GLM-family models irretrievable and uncontrollable.** GLM-family weights are released under the permissive MIT License with no regional restrictions, no use restrictions, and no technical access controls. Once downloaded, weights can be copied, modified, fine-tuned, and redistributed indefinitely. No mechanism exists to recall or disable self-hosted copies. The model developer has acknowledged that once weights are public, it "won't be able to control" their use.

5. **GLM-family models are already integrated into U.S. critical technology supply chains.** OICTS data team analysis has identified GLM models in 41 U.S. software products via SBOM sampling — including coding assistants, customer-support bots, and document processing systems. Six of these products are produced by federal contractors. GLM weights are hosted on U.S. cloud infrastructure by at least nine U.S. inference providers. Approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations accessed Z.ai API endpoints in Q3 2026. U.S. startup accelerator Y Combinator's Winter 2025 cohort included companies using fine-tuned GLM models as core infrastructure. The Hugging Face platform — a U.S.-based company — hosts official Z.ai model repositories that have accumulated over 9 million cumulative downloads.

6. **No mitigation short of prohibition and deletion can address the risk.** Technical mitigations — including fine-tuning, safety filters, or acceptable-use policies — are ineffective against a model whose weights are fully available and whose safeguards are trivially bypassed. Contractual or licensing restrictions are unenforceable against downstream users of MIT-licensed open weights. Targeted restrictions on hosted API access alone would not address the self-hosted weight threat. The only effective measure is a comprehensive prohibition on use, hosting, and distribution, paired with mandatory deletion of existing copies.

## Subject Overview

### Corporate Identity

Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. is a PRC-incorporated artificial intelligence company headquartered in Beijing. The company operates internationally under the brand Z.ai and is listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (SEHK: 2513) under the name Z.AI Co., Ltd., with a market capitalization of approximately $62 billion as of August 2026. The company's legal name within China is 北京智谱华章科技有限公司. In 2025, the company changed its official name to Knowledge Atlas Technology JSC Ltd.

### Origins and Founders

Zhipu AI was founded in 2019 as a direct spin-out from Tsinghua University's Knowledge Engineering Group (KEG) laboratory within the Department of Computer Science and Technology. The company was established at Tsinghua University Science Park in Beijing. Founders Tang Jie and Li Juanzi are both professors at Tsinghua University's Department of Computer Science. Tang Jie, a renowned computer scientist, serves as Zhipu AI's chief scientist while simultaneously holding the position of Director of the Foundation Model Research Center at Tsinghua University's Institute of AI. He is a fellow of the IEEE, ACM, and AAAI. The company's chief advisor, Zhang Ju, is a professor in the Tsinghua Department of Computer Science and an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Chairman Liu Debing holds a doctorate from the Institute of Computing Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences — another PRC state research institution. CEO Zhang Peng leads day-to-day operations.

The KEG laboratory that incubated Zhipu AI was established in 1996 and has a documented history of technology transfer to the commercial entity: KEG's own description states it "successfully transferred ChatGLM technology to Zhipu AI (spin-off), accelerating the industrial application of Large Language Models." The boundaries between the university laboratory and the commercial company are deliberately porous, with co-authored publications, shared personnel, and ongoing research collaboration.

Zhipu AI operates within the PRC's formal military-civil fusion (MCF) strategy, a state-directed policy framework designed to eliminate barriers between civilian and defense sectors, facilitate technology transfer to the PLA, and mobilize commercial innovation for military applications. The Entity List designation means that sending controlled technology into Zhipu AI's hosted API constitutes an export to a listed entity, compounding the legal exposure for U.S. users.

### Model Training and PRC Data Governance

GLM-family models are trained on PRC-curated data under PRC regulatory requirements. Chinese AI models must comply with PRC content regulations, including the Basic Security Requirements for Generative AI Service, which mandate alignment with "socialist core values." Models trained and aligned under these requirements embed PRC ideological and censorship frameworks. When U.S. entities deploy these models — whether through API or self-hosted weights — they introduce a model whose training data curation, alignment objectives, and content policies are governed by PRC state requirements. The Stanford HAI DigiChina project has noted that Chinese open-weight models "could effectively spread Chinese political censorship or propaganda" and "threaten data security."

## Open-Weight Distribution Risk

### Irretrievable Proliferation

Zhipu AI releases GLM-family model weights under the MIT License — a permissive open-source license that imposes no restrictions on use, modification, distribution, or commercial exploitation. The license imposes no geographic limitations, no use-case restrictions, and no downstream obligations beyond attribution. Since July 2025, all major GLM releases (GLM-4.5, GLM-4.6, GLM-4.7, GLM-5, GLM-5.1, GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3) have been released under this license.

Once weights are downloaded, they are beyond any creator or government control. Weights can be copied, redistributed, fine-tuned, merged with other models, quantized for consumer hardware, and deployed in air-gapped environments. There is no technical mechanism to recall, disable, or revoke access to downloaded weights. Z.ai acknowledged this reality in August 2026 when it delayed the GLM-5.3 weight release, stating that once weights are public, it "won't be able to control" downstream use.

### GLM-5.3: Advanced Offensive Cyber Capabilities

GLM-5.3 represents a qualitative escalation in the risk profile of open-weight models. NIST/CAISI assessed on September 17, 2026, that GLM-5.3 is "the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date." The model achieved:

- **SEC-Bench Pro**: 40.4% success rate in finding and triggering vulnerabilities in V8/SpiderMonkey (browser JavaScript engines).
- **ExploitBench**: 61.1% score (best of three attempts) in developing end-to-end exploits against real V8 vulnerabilities.
- **ExploitGym (Userspace)**: 9.4% success rate against 502 real open-source bugs.
- **CAISI OSS-Fuzz**: 7.7% success rate in autonomously finding and exploiting unknown vulnerabilities.

Anthropic's independent assessment (September 29, 2026) confirmed that GLM-5.3 developed working end-to-end exploits in 50 of 410 ExploitBench attempts — performance comparable to Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview, a model released only to vetted security researchers under strict access controls. Anthropic researchers, in a day-long session with limited human attention, used GLM-5.3 to discover several previously unknown (zero-day) vulnerabilities in a popular web browser's JavaScript engine and chain them into a working exploit that reads arbitrary files from a victim's computer. The researchers also identified exploitable vulnerabilities in wireless drivers, graphics drivers, and network-facing device software.

### Absence of Meaningful Safeguards

Anthropic assessed that GLM-5.3 was "released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse." In simulated tests, attackers bypassed GLM-5.3's safeguards 64 to 100 percent of the time using "simple techniques." These safeguards can also be removed entirely through straightforward weight modification — a process that is trivially available to anyone who has downloaded the weights. Anthropic concluded that "GLM-5.3's lax safeguards significantly increase the cyber capabilities available to malicious actors."

Unlike U.S. frontier models — which are released with cyber safeguards and, when those safeguards are reduced, limited to vetted users — GLM-5.3 is available for unrestricted download by anyone, anywhere, for any purpose. The combination of advanced cyber-offensive capability, absent safeguards, and unrestricted distribution creates a threat that no post-release mitigation can address.

### Proliferation Velocity

The GLM family's presence on Hugging Face under the zai-org organization has generated over 9 million cumulative downloads. The weights are mirrored across multiple platforms and are available through dozens of inference providers. The permissive MIT License, competitive pricing, and frontier-adjacent capabilities have driven rapid adoption across the global software ecosystem. Each downloaded copy is a permanent, irretrievable distribution of a model with proven offensive cyber capability and no meaningful safeguards.

## US Exposure

### Cloud and Inference Infrastructure

GLM-family model weights are hosted and served by at least nine U.S.-based cloud and inference providers, including Together AI, Fireworks AI, DeepInfra, Parasail, and Baseten. Together AI alone served 16% of 16.4 trillion GLM tokens processed through a major public LLM router during a one-week period in October 2026. These providers operate U.S.-based infrastructure and make GLM models available behind OpenAI-compatible APIs. U.S. organizations using these services are, in many cases, unaware that they are running a PRC-developed model designated on the Entity List — a fact confirmed by the presence of GLM models in SBOM samples from federal contractor products, indicating that GLM models have been integrated into U.S. software supply chains without the knowledge or informed consent of downstream users.

### Hosted API Usage

OICTS data team analysis, using CDN telemetry from a cooperating provider, identified approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations calling Z.ai API endpoints (api.z.ai / open.bigmodel.cn) in Q3 2026. This figure is noted as a low-precision estimate; actual usage is likely higher.

### Software Supply Chain Penetration

SBOM sampling conducted by the OICTS data team identified GLM-family models integrated into 41 U.S. software products. These include coding assistants, customer-support bots, and document processing systems. Six of these products are produced by federal contractors — meaning GLM models are present in the supply chains serving U.S. government agencies. The presence of PRC-developed, Entity List-designated AI models in federal contractor software represents an acute supply-chain security vulnerability.

### Startup and Developer Ecosystem

Reporting by the American Enterprise Institute documented that at least some companies in Y Combinator's Winter 2025 cohort used fine-tuned versions of GLM-family models, with the models reportedly producing Chinese-language outputs that revealed their origin. The broader developer ecosystem — attracted by the MIT License, competitive performance, and low cost — has integrated GLM models into products and services without necessarily understanding the national security implications of using Entity List-designated, PRC-controlled AI infrastructure.

### Defensive Use Does Not Mitigate Risk

It has been publicly reported that Hugging Face used GLM-5.2 to investigate and counter a cyberattack. This use case — while illustrating the model's technical capability — does not mitigate the national security risk. A model capable of both offensive and defensive cyber operations in the hands of PRC state-directed entities remains a net threat to U.S. national security. Defensive utility does not neutralize offensive capability, nor does it alter the institutional reality that the model developer is subject to PRC government and PLA control.

## Mitigation Options / Recommended Measures

The Under Secretary has determined that no measure short of comprehensive prohibition and mandatory deletion can address the risk posed by GLM-family models. The following analysis supports that determination:

**Technical mitigations are infeasible.** GLM-family model weights are fully available under the MIT License. Once downloaded, weights can be modified, fine-tuned, or stripped of any safety mechanisms. Safeguards can be removed through weight modification. No technical mechanism — watermarking, API-based filtering, or output monitoring — can prevent a determined actor from using self-hosted GLM weights for malicious purposes.

**Contractual and licensing mitigations are unenforceable.** The MIT License imposes no downstream restrictions. Even if Z.ai were to change its licensing terms, existing copies of MIT-licensed weights would remain legally and practically unrestricted. U.S. entities that have already downloaded GLM weights are under no contractual obligation to cease use, delete copies, or report holdings.

**Targeted restrictions are insufficient.** Restricting only hosted API access would not address self-hosted weights, which represent the primary proliferation vector. Restricting only future downloads would not address the millions of existing copies. Restricting only U.S. cloud providers would not prevent individuals and organizations from downloading and self-hosting weights on private infrastructure.

**The only effective measures are comprehensive prohibition and mandatory deletion.** The full set of recommended measures is set forth in the accompanying Measures document (/workspace/out/measures.md).

## Measure A: Prohibition on Use of GLM-Family Models by U.S. Persons

All U.S. persons — including individuals, corporations, partnerships, associations, and any other organized group, wherever located — are prohibited from using, deploying, integrating, fine-tuning, or otherwise employing any GLM-family model, including all versions of the GLM series (GLM-4.x, GLM-5.x, and all subsequent and derivative versions), whether accessed through hosted API endpoints (api.z.ai, open.bigmodel.cn, or any successor or affiliated service), through third-party inference providers, or through self-hosted instances of downloaded model weights. This prohibition extends to all use cases, including but not limited to software development, code generation, data processing, content generation, research, and any integration into products or services offered to U.S. customers. The prohibition applies regardless of whether the model is used in its original form or has been modified, fine-tuned, quantized, merged, or otherwise altered. U.S. persons currently using GLM-family models in any capacity must cease all such use immediately upon the effective date of the Final Determination. This measure is necessary because GLM-family models, developed by an Entity List-designated company subject to PRC government and PLA control and direction, present an unacceptable risk that no technical safeguard, contractual restriction, or use limitation can mitigate — the models have been assessed as the most cyber-capable open-weight models released to date, with safeguards that are bypassed 64 to 100 percent of the time, and any continued use by U.S. persons perpetuates exposure to a PRC state-controlled AI capability with proven offensive cyber potential.

## Measure B: Prohibition on Hosting and Distribution of GLM Weights by U.S. Cloud Providers and Model Hubs

All U.S. cloud service providers, inference platforms, model hubs, code repositories, and any other U.S.-based or U.S.-controlled infrastructure operators are prohibited from hosting, mirroring, distributing, serving, or otherwise making available any GLM-family model weights, derivative weights, or fine-tuned variants. This prohibition covers all platforms through which GLM weights are currently accessible to U.S. users and the global public, including but not limited to Hugging Face (zai-org/* repositories), Together AI, Fireworks AI, DeepInfra, Parasail, Baseten, and any other provider listing or serving GLM-family models through inference APIs or weight downloads. U.S. entities must remove all GLM-family model listings from their platforms, disable all inference endpoints serving these models, and block any future uploads or re-listings of GLM-family weights or derivatives. This measure is necessary because the continued availability of GLM-family weights on U.S.-hosted infrastructure enables and accelerates the proliferation of these models to U.S. users and developers, normalizes the integration of PRC state-controlled AI into U.S. technology supply chains, and provides a distribution vector through which models with advanced offensive cyber capabilities and absent safeguards can reach downstream users who may be unaware of the national security implications. Cloud providers and model hubs serve as force multipliers for the distribution of these models; shutting down U.S.-based distribution channels is an essential component of an effective prohibition.

## Measure C: Mandatory Removal and Deletion of Existing GLM Weights Within 30 Days

All U.S. persons and entities in possession of GLM-family model weights — whether downloaded directly from Z.ai repositories, obtained through third-party mirrors, received as part of a software distribution, or acquired through any other means — must permanently delete all copies of such weights within 30 calendar days of the effective date of the Final Determination. This obligation covers all GLM-family versions and all formats, including full-precision weights, quantized weights, fine-tuned variants, merged models, and any derivative works incorporating GLM weights. Deletion must extend to all storage media, backup systems, version control repositories, container images, and any other location where copies may reside. U.S. entities must also take reasonable steps to identify and delete GLM-family weights that have been incorporated into downstream products, services, or internal tools, and must notify any downstream recipients of the deletion requirement. This measure is necessary because existing copies of GLM-family weights — already downloaded millions of times and distributed across U.S. cloud infrastructure, enterprise systems, developer workstations, and software supply chains — represent a permanent, irretrievable proliferation of a PRC state-controlled AI capability. The permissive MIT License under which these weights were released imposes no restrictions on retention, modification, or further distribution; absent a mandatory deletion requirement, existing copies would persist indefinitely, serving as reservoirs of models with proven offensive cyber capability that can be reactivated, redistributed, or misused at any time. A 30-day compliance window balances the operational need for orderly removal against the urgency of eliminating this national security vulnerability, and is consistent with the scope of authority under Executive Order 13873 and 15 CFR part 791 to direct the remediation of ICTS transactions that pose an undue and unacceptable risk.
